$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}F(x), & x\in [0,\pi ), \\ F(-x), & x\in (-\pi ,0).\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =F(-x) \\  & =(-x)^{2}-2(-x) \\  & ={x}^{2}+2x.\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
Let $F(x)=2x+3$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ Select the correct missing parts in the Fourier cosine series of the **even** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function $F(x)$ below.

$$
f(x)∼(3+\pi )+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot {{field-2}}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=2x+3$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2x+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=2x+3\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=2 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{2}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(\frac{1}{n}[(2x+3)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{2}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(((2\pi +3)\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\frac{2}{n}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(0+\frac{2}{n}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{4(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-1)}{{n}^{2}\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{4((-1)^{n}-1)}{\pi {n}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, the Fourier cosine series is

$$
f(x)∼(3+\pi )+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{4((-1)^{n}-1)}{\pi {n}^{2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(nx).
$$

$$

Let $F(x)=-3x$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ The Fourier cosine series of the **even** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the expression for ${a}_{n}.$

$\,{a}_{n}=$ {{field-1}}
for $n\ge 1$
questions.worked_solution:
For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-3x$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{a}_{n}=-\frac{6}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }x\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =-\frac{6}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{6}{\pi }(\frac{1}{n}[x\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{1}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{6}{n\pi }((\pi \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\frac{1}{n}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =-\frac{6}{n\pi }(0+\frac{1}{n}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{6(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi ))}{{n}^{2}\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{6(1-(-1)^{n})}{\pi {n}^{2}}.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Let $F(x)=x^3 - x + 5\cos x$ for $x\in[0,\pi),$ and let $f(x)$ be the **even** extension of $F(x)$ to $x \in (-\pi,\pi).$ What is $f(x)$ for $x\in(-\pi,0)?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in[0,\pi),$ the even extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121869/assets/9d4ae844370b06d82ce892e052ecd1c114519a6bb31e153e3bcb10c2c4806d56.svg)

In our cases, for $x\in(-\pi,0),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =F(-x) \\  & =(-x)^{3}-(-x)+5\operatorname{cos}⁡(-x) \\  & =-{x}^{3}+x+5\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
$$
f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n \cos(nx)
$$

Let $F(x)=\sin\left(\dfrac{3x}{4}\right)$ for $x\in[0,\pi).$ The Fourier cosine series of the **even** $2\pi$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the expression for $a_0.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For our Fourier cosine series, the constant term is given by

$$
a_0=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\sin\left(\dfrac{3x}{4}\right)$ for $x \in (0,\pi).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3x}{4})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }{[-\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3x}{4})]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-\frac{8}{3\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\frac{8}{3\pi }(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-1) \\  & =\frac{4}{3\pi }(\sqrt{2}+2).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Computing the Cosine Coefficients From the Half-Range Formula
canonical_examples.problem:
Let $F(x)=-6x-2$ for $x\in[0,\pi).$ Find the missing parts in the Fourier cosine series of the **even** $2\pi$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function $F(x).$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121869/assets/4f5284fb6fed9d16cafa85a546e65db1b9ebf5a5211d870b24dfe87bb1ccb49b.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
a_n=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(x)\cos(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-6x-2$ for $x \in (0,\pi).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
a_n = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi (-6x-2) \cos(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=-6x-2\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=-6 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{2}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(\frac{1}{n}[(-6x-2)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{6}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(((-6\pi -2)\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))-\frac{6}{n}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(0-\frac{6}{n}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{12(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi ))}{{n}^{2}\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\cos(n\pi)=(-1)^n,$ we have

$$
a_n = \dfrac{12(1-(-1)^n)}{\pi n^2}.
$$

Finally, the Fourier cosine series is

$$
f(x) \sim (-2-3\pi) + \sum_{n=1}^\infty 
\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{12(1-(-1)^n)}{\pi n^2}} 
\cdot 
\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\cos(nx)}.
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
In the earlier topics, we saw that *symmetry* can force many Fourier coefficients to be zero automatically.
In particular, if a $2\pi$-periodic function is *even*, then its Fourier series has *cosine terms only*.

A **Fourier cosine series** uses this idea when a function is initially given only on the half-interval $[0,\pi),$ but we want a full Fourier series on $[-\pi,\pi)$ (and then a $2\pi$-periodic extension to all real $x$).

To do this, we start with a function $F(x)$ on $[0,\pi)$ and define its **even extension** $f(x)$ to $(-\pi,\pi)$ by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121869/assets/e2e07048ac4750968947e45443f59096f395b159d4f7a846410a711194b11a14.svg)

For example, a function $F(x),$ defined on $x \in [0,1),$ and its even extension $f(x)$ to $x \in (-1,1)$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121869/assets/33d92f280a5672c8d9d94553ccc1ada2a9c5ea1ff12344ca8c9aeca9f44c40c6.png)

By construction, $f$ is an *even* function, meaning $f(-x)=f(x)$. Because $f$ is even, its Fourier series on $[-\pi,\pi)$ has *cosine terms only*:

$$
f(x)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\cos(nx)
$$

Since $f(x)$ is even and $\cos(nx)$ is even for any $n\ge 1,$ the product $f(x)\cos(nx)$ is even too. Therefore, the cosine coefficients can be computed using the *half-range formulas*:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot 2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and for $n\ge 1,$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot 2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

So in practice, the workflow is the following:

- Start with $F$ on $[0,\pi)$ and form the even extension $f$ on $(-\pi,\pi).$

- Compute $a_0$ and $a_n$ from the half-range integrals on $[0,\pi).$

- Write the Fourier cosine series of $f.$

Let's see some concrete examples.
